title: ¿Puedo coger el micro?  (Can I Borrow the Mic?)

segments.t: Up on the Primera Fila stage, rival agent Fernando Canelón praises the drama students and quietly slips his business card to Mariona. Refusing to be outdone, Paquita climbs up, borrows the microphone, and congratulates the cast on behalf of PS Management. Listen to the Spanish first, then we'll walk through each line.
Muchas gracias. Enhorabuena a todos.
Habéis estado fantásticos.
Te doy mi tarjeta por si te escapas.
Todos están muy bien, pero tú estás brillante.
Uno sale al escenario y ve lo difícil que es ser actor.
Perdón, una cosita. ¿Puedo coger el micro un momento?
Gracias. Perdón por la intrusión.
Yo soy Paquita Salas, de PS Management.
También soy representante de actores.
Chicos, enhorabuena por el curro.
Pido un aplauso para ellos otra vez, por favor.
Let's hear how Fernando praises the cast and how Paquita steps in.
Muchas gracias. Enhorabuena a todos.

'Thank you very much. Congratulations to everyone.' Spain's favourite single word for "congratulations" is built from three pieces that literally mean "in a good hour". Adding "to all" directs the praise to the whole group onstage.
Habéis estado fantásticos.

'You've been fantastic.' Addressing the students as a group in Spain uses the informal plural form of "you have". Notice the masculine plural ending on "fantastic", which covers a mixed group of men and women.
Te doy mi tarjeta por si te escapas.

'I'm giving you my card in case you slip away.' That neat two-word link in the middle literally says "for if" and works just like English "just in case". At the end, "you escape" playfully imagines Mariona sneaking off before they talk.
Todos están muy bien, pero tú estás brillante.

'Everyone is very good, but you're brilliant.' Rather than the permanent "be", Fernando chooses the state form here because he means how they performed tonight, not their personalities in general. He includes the explicit word for "you" to single Mariona out from the rest.
Uno sale al escenario y ve lo difícil que es ser actor.

'You step out onto the stage and see how hard it is to be an actor.' Where casual English says "you step out", Spanish often uses "one goes out" for people in general. Before "stage", "to" and "the" fuse into one short word, and a neuter article before "difficult" builds "how hard it is".
Perdón, una cosita. ¿Puedo coger el micro un momento?

'Excuse me, just one little thing. Can I borrow the mic for a moment?' Softening "thing" with a diminutive ending makes Paquita's interruption sound harmless and polite. In Peninsular Spanish, the everyday word for "take" or "grab" is completely normal here, and "microphone" clips down to two syllables.
Gracias. Perdón por la intrusión.

'Thank you. Sorry for the intrusion.' After "pardon", Spanish links the reason with "for", matching English "sorry for" word for word. "Intrusion" sounds almost like its English cousin, just stressed right on the final syllable.
Yo soy Paquita Salas, de PS Management.

'I'm Paquita Salas, from PS Management.' Usually Spaniards drop the word for "I", since "am" already reveals who is speaking. Keeping it right at the start puts extra spotlight on Paquita as she introduces herself after Fernando.
También soy representante de actores.

'I'm also a talent agent for actors.' Opening with "also" reminds the hall that Fernando is not the only agent in the room. Once again, Spanish skips "a" before the job title and links "actors" with "of" rather than "for".
Chicos, enhorabuena por el curro.

'Kids, congratulations on the hard work.' Addressing young adults affectionately as "boys and girls" is standard across Spain. At the end, Paquita reaches for a lively Madrid slang noun meaning "work" or "graft" instead of the textbook word.
Pido un aplauso para ellos otra vez, por favor.

'I ask for another round of applause for them, please.' The opening action word packs "ask for" into one piece, so you never add a separate "for" right after it; "for them" introduces the recipients instead. At the close, "other time" is the natural Spanish chunk for "again". Now let's listen to the whole scene again.
Muchas gracias. Enhorabuena a todos.
Habéis estado fantásticos.
Te doy mi tarjeta por si te escapas.
Todos están muy bien, pero tú estás brillante.
Uno sale al escenario y ve lo difícil que es ser actor.
Perdón, una cosita. ¿Puedo coger el micro un momento?
Gracias. Perdón por la intrusión.
Yo soy Paquita Salas, de PS Management.
También soy representante de actores.
Chicos, enhorabuena por el curro.
Pido un aplauso para ellos otra vez, por favor.
You heard warm Spanish congratulations, two ways to say "be" side by side, and Spain's everyday slang word for hard work. See you next time.
¡Hasta luego!
